4. Language ID: what sits on the 0.65 line

The problem. An English corpus must drop other languages, and the crawl does not label them reliably. How it works. fastText's lid.176 is a linear classifier over averaged character n-gram embeddings: it turns the text (newlines replaced by spaces, utils/lid.py:54) into a probability for each of 176 languages. datatrove keeps a document when the English probability exceeds 0.65 (filters/language_filter.py:61-65), FineWeb's threshold. Cost: microseconds per document on a CPU, which is why it runs before every rule. How to check it: read what lands near the threshold.

English probability for the 19,241 documents trafilatura extracted (lid.176, measured). Most mass sits at the two ends; the slider moves the cut.

Top languages of the extracted documents
Pages just around the threshold
What the boundary is made of

Every page shown between 0.52 and 0.82 (a random sample of organisation pages, seed 0) is in English. What lowers the score is not another language but text that is not prose: menus, search facets, data tables, a PHP error log, OCR of a scanned newspaper. lid.176 was trained on running text (Wikipedia, Tatoeba and SETimes, per the fastText language-identification page), so a list of short labels looks less like any language. The 0.65 threshold therefore also acts as a weak quality filter, and the rule filters after it remove most of these pages anyway.

The trap in the shipped example, and a default that changed under it

5. Heuristic rule explorer

The problem. After language ID, most English pages are still not prose worth training on. How it works. Each rule computes one number from the text and compares it with a threshold; the Gopher, C4 and FineWeb rule sets run in that order and the first rule that fires removes the document. Pick a rule, move its threshold, and see how many of the 6,971 English documents it would drop on its own, how many it drops among documents that pass every other rule (its real effect in the chain), and how many of those FineWeb itself kept. Real documents on both sides of the threshold are listed under the chart (short excerpts, scrubbed of emails).

Dropped at the default threshold

Kept, closest to the threshold (organisations)

Labels on dropped documents: right a careful curator would drop it too, wrong coherent, informative prose, unclear. Labelled by the agent that built this tab from the first few hundred characters (one reader; see section 6).

Predict: datatrove's FineWeb filter drops a document when more than 0.01 of its characters sit in duplicated lines. The FineWeb paper says 0.1. If you used 0.1, how many more of the 6,971 documents would survive the whole chain?

6. Right and wrong drops, labelled

A filter's drop count says nothing about whether it drops the right documents. The only check is to read a sample. For every rule that removed documents, 8 documents it removed were drawn at random (seed 0; all of them when fewer), plus 24 documents the whole chain kept, and each was labelled from its first 360 to 700 characters. Labels are committed in src/pipe/labels/drops.json. Eight per rule is enough to see a pattern, not to estimate a rate: treat one wrong drop in eight as "happens", six in eight as "the rule is broken at this threshold".

7. PII scrubbing: what two regular expressions catch and miss

The problem. Web text contains personal data: email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, names. A model can memorise and repeat it. How it works in FineWeb. datatrove's PIIFormatter (pipeline/formatters/pii.py:42-94) runs two regular expressions: one for email addresses (replaced in turn by email@example.com and firstname.lastname@example.org) and one for IPv4 addresses, replaced only when Python's ipaddress says they are global (pii.py:34-39), so 192.168.x.x and other private addresses stay. Nothing else is touched. Cost: two regex passes per document; nothing is removed, text is edited.

Caught (run0, 2,617 documents)
Still there after scrubbing (simple detectors written for this lab)

The same text before and after, constructed example (not from the crawl)
When it matters and how to check it

Regex scrubbing is cheap and predictable, which is why FineWeb uses it; its limits are in the counts above. Phone numbers, street addresses and social handles remain, and almost half of what the email regex replaces (66 of 140) are role addresses of organisations (info@, sales@), not people. Stronger options cost more: NER-based tools such as Microsoft Presidio find names and addresses, with false positives of their own, and one way to afford them is to run them only on the higher-risk slices (forums, comments). To check a scrubber, count matches of independent detectors after it, as here, and read a sample.

8. Read the source: how datatrove runs a pipeline

Everything above is a handful of Python classes. Reading them is the fastest way to know what a pipeline really does (all paths under src/datatrove/, tag v0.10.1, commit 1977fbb0).

  • A pipeline is a list of steps, and documents stream through it. Each step is a PipelineStep whose run(data, rank, world_size) (pipeline/base.py:99) takes a generator of Document objects and yields documents; the executor chains them, so nothing is held in memory between steps. A reader is the first step and ignores its input.
  • Filters subclass BaseFilter: filter(doc) returns True or (False, reason); the base class counts the reason in its stats and, if given an exclusion_writer, writes the dropped document with metadata.filter_reason (pipeline/filters/base_filter.py:62-82). That is how every removed document in this tab could be read back.
  • Extractors run each page in a sandboxed subprocess with a wall-clock timeout (pipeline/extractors/base.py:40-65, the sandbox class at line 85; trafilatura's options at extractors/trafilatura.py:22-55). On macOS the sandbox needs the fork start method, one of the workarounds in this lab's scripts.
  • The executor splits input files into tasks (FineWeb used 8,000 per crawl on a Slurm cluster, examples/fineweb.py:65); each task writes its own output shard and a stats JSON, which is where the per-stage counts in section 1 come from. The same pipeline runs locally (LocalPipelineExecutor), on Slurm or on Ray, which is why a laptop run reproduces the cluster run per document.
  • MinHash is four pipeline stages (signatures, buckets, clustering, filtering) because each needs all the output of the previous one: see the Dedup lab.

Each rule's file and line range is shown under the rule explorer chart; language ID at filters/language_filter.py:43-65 and utils/lid.py:53-59; URL filter at filters/url_filter.py:80-132.

9. Common mistakes, and interview questions

Trusting a library default or an example script
The datatrove FineWeb example became multilingual when a default changed (section 4); its quality filter uses 0.01 where the paper says 0.1, and C4's sentence minimum is 5 where the T5 paper says 3 (section 5). Pin versions, pass every argument that matters, and diff your output against a known reference (here, FineWeb's own documents from the same file: 2,403 of 2,425 reproduced).
Using WET text because it is already extracted
Measured here: 877 English documents survive the filters from WET text against 2,692 from trafilatura on the same pages. WET's menus and widgets make the repetition and line rules fire, and what survives carries boilerplate. FineWeb (trafilatura) and DCLM (resiliparse) both re-extract from WARC.
Letting machine load change the dataset
A per-page timeout depends on wall-clock time, so a busy node drops more pages: 199 timeouts in run0, 12 of which FineWeb kept. Size timeouts generously, log them as a stage, and rerun them.
Reading a drop count as a quality measure
A rule that removes 173 documents can be wrong on most of them (the 0.01 duplicated-line rule: 6 wrong of 8 labelled). Label a sample on each side of every threshold before trusting it.
Tuning thresholds on one file and calling it done
One WARC cannot show cross-file duplication, and rare rules (lorem ipsum, curly brackets) fire a handful of times. Check a decision on several files and, for dedup, on the whole crawl.
Calling regex scrubbing "PII removal"
Two regexes catch emails and public IPs only; phone numbers, addresses and names remain (section 7). Say exactly what was scrubbed.

Interview questions, with short answers

Why does the URL filter run before extraction, and language ID before the quality rules?
Cheapest first: each stage should remove as much as it can before a more expensive one runs. A URL lookup costs microseconds and reads no content; extraction costs milliseconds per page; language ID is cheap and removes about 64% of extracted documents in a crawl like this; spaCy-tokenised rules and neural classifiers are the most expensive, so they see the least.
FineWeb's WET ablation lost to trafilatura on WARC. Why, mechanically?
WET keeps every visible string, so documents carry navigation, cookie banners and widget text. That both adds low-value tokens and changes the statistics the filters see (duplicate lines, short lines, lines without punctuation), so some good pages are dropped and many bad ones survive. On our file the same filters keep 877 documents from WET against 2,692 from trafilatura.
How would you choose a threshold for a new heuristic rule?
FineWeb's method: compare the rule's distribution on a high-quality and a low-quality reference (they used their dedup ablations), pick a cut where they separate, then train small models on data with and without the rule and compare benchmark scores. Before that, label a sample of what it drops near the threshold, and report the share of tokens it removes.
Your pipeline's output differs from a published dataset built with the same code. Where do you look?
Versions and defaults (library and model versions, changed defaults), arguments the example omits, extraction timeouts and failures, dedup scope (per file, per crawl, global), and order of stages. Join on a stable id (here WARC-Record-ID) and inspect the documents in one set and not the other, stage by stage.
Design: you have one week of CPU to turn one Common Crawl crawl into an English pretraining set. What runs where?
Read WARCs from object storage in many parallel tasks (one shard of files per task); per document, in order: URL blocklist, extraction (resiliparse if CPU is the constraint, about 8 times faster per DCLM; trafilatura if precision matters more), lid.176, repetition and quality rules, PII regexes, writing the survivors with their stats; then MinHash per crawl as a separate multi-stage job; then a model-based quality classifier on the survivors (GPU if available). Keep every removed document with its reason, a stats file per task, and a labelled sample per rule.

Scripts, data and labels: src/pipe/ in this page's folder (see its README). Measured on Apple M1 Pro (CPU), 2026-10-14; per-document results transfer to a cluster exactly (same code, same inputs), timings do not.

The same web text appears many times: syndicated articles, mirrors, templates, and, above all, boilerplate. This lab runs every deduplication method a pretraining pipeline uses on the page's running example (one Common Crawl WARC file of CC-MAIN-2024-30, taken through a FineWeb-style datatrove pipeline as run0) and shows what each one removes, why, and what it costs.

Labels used below: measured on the running example on an Apple M1 Pro (CPU) on 2026-10-14; published by the authors (their scale, not rerun here); derived from a formula; vendor claims. Timings are rough (a shared machine, 4 threads, low priority).

At a glanceExactMinHash and LSHClustersSuffix arraysBloom filtersSemanticAcross crawlsCostSourceCheck yourself

At a glance: five methods on the same 2,692 documents

The input is run0's filtered stage: the 2,692 English documents from our WARC that passed every heuristic filter, exactly what datatrove's MinHash step received. Each method was run on all of them; the bars count documents a method removes outright (the suffix-array row counts documents that lose at least half their bytes).

measured Exact: identical text, first copy kept. MinHash: datatrove 0.10.1 with FineWeb's settings (5-word shingles, 14 bands of 8 hashes), the same 75 documents run0 removed. C4 spans: datatrove's SentenceDedup (drop every repeated three-sentence span, then drop documents left with fewer than 3 sentences or 50 words). Suffix arrays: Google's deduplicate-text-datasets, repeated spans of 100 bytes or more, every copy removed. Semantic: SemDeDup's rule with an arctic-embed-m encoder, cosine at least 0.9.

The same documents before and after each method

Fourteen of the 2,692, picked to show where the methods disagree. Each card is one document (hostname, the start of its text after PII scrubbing). Every cluster here includes the copy a method keeps, except semantic dedup, whose kept copy of the banner sits outside this set. Fates come from the full run on all 2,692 documents.

What the animation shows
Most of what MinHash removes on a single crawl file is not "the same article twice" but boilerplate that survived extraction: 25 documents whose extracted text is only a cookie banner. Exact hashing catches byte-identical copies only; MinHash also catches the banner with an extra heading, and through chaining (A is close to B, B to C) it also removed the stove page, which had two sentences of real text. Suffix arrays remove the shared span inside every copy, keeping none, and leave the stove sentences. Semantic dedup is the only one that pairs the two casino spam articles, which share almost no 5-word phrases.

Exact dedup: hashes of documents, lines and sentence spans

Why bother at all (the Reading tab's section 1 table and Deduplication, section 1, have the evidence): repeats waste training compute, make a model memorise (a 1.5B model trained on C4 emitted memorised text in 1.9% of its output tokens, 0.19% after near-duplicate removal; published Lee et al. 2021, Table 4), and copy benchmark items. Muennighoff et al. found up to about 4 repeats nearly as good as fresh data, so dedup is mostly about not spending the budget twice on the same boilerplate.

The idea. Compute a hash (a short fingerprint, here 64 bits, so equal inputs give equal fingerprints and different inputs almost never collide) of each unit, sort or group by it, keep one per value. The unit decides what you catch:

measured Three run0 stages: extracted (19,241 documents straight out of Trafilatura, every language), filtered (2,692, after language ID and the Gopher, C4 and FineWeb rules) and final (2,617, after MinHash). "Normalised" hashes datatrove's simplify_text (lowercase, no punctuation, numbers normalised). Lines follow the Dolma toolkit's paragraph loop: split on newlines, skip blank ones, keep the first copy. No URL appears twice in one WARC file: Common Crawl deduplicates URLs within a crawl, so URL dedup only matters across crawls.

Predict, then check the table
On the raw extracted text, what fraction of non-blank lines are an exact repeat of a line seen earlier in the same file? (the answer is in the table: lines row, extracted column) Many are menu items and separators ("Home", "Contact Us", "|"), which is why line dedup on raw text is aggressive: it also strips table separators and list markers that carry structure.

The lines most often repeated across different sites

measured on the 19,241 extracted documents; only lines seen on at least 5 different hosts are listed, so none is one site's own text. 3,503 distinct lines qualify, with 111,609 occurrences between them. Short lines are navigation and table markup; among lines of 40 characters or more, consent-plugin text dominates: the extractor kept the cookie banner as if it were content.

C4's rule: every repeated three-sentence span

C4 "discarded all but one of any three-sentence span occurring more than once" (Raffel et al. 2020). datatrove implements it as SentenceDedup: split each document into sentences, hash every window of 3 consecutive sentences after normalising, mark windows seen before, cut them, then drop documents left with fewer than 3 sentences or 50 words.

measured datatrove 0.10.1 SentenceDedupSignature, SentenceFindDedups and SentenceDedupFilter with n_sentences=3, min_doc_words=50, on run0's filtered (before MinHash) and final (after MinHash) stages. Of the 70 documents it drops before MinHash, 64 are also among MinHash's 75 and all 50 exact copies are among them: on whole-document duplicates the methods agree; the span rule adds the 24 documents it shortens. A trap in the code: SentenceDedupSignature.__init__ reads config.hash_config from its argument (sentence_dedup.py:96), so leaving config at its default None crashes; pass a SentDedupConfig.

MinHash and LSH, measured on every pair

Deduplication, section 3, explains the four steps (shingles, Jaccard, the min-hash trick, bands and rows) with a stepper and draws the S-curve in its Band designer; the Reading tab's section 4 defines them in a line. Here the curve meets real pairs. Among 2,692 documents there are 3,622,086 pairs. For every one of them we computed the true Jaccard similarity of the shingle sets (a sparse matrix product, no estimate) and compared datatrove's 112 MinHash values position by position.

measured Shingles and signatures recomputed with datatrove's own MinhashDedupSignature code; all 37,688 stored signature values (2,692 documents by 14 bands) equal run0's signature files, and union-find over the candidates reproduces run0's 31 clusters and its 75 removals. Only 19,675 pairs share even one shingle; 856 pairs have a Jaccard of at least 0.05 or at least 2 equal MinHash values, and every other pair has at most one equal value, so it can never become a candidate when a band has 2 or more rows. Those 856 pairs, with their 112-position equality masks, are embedded in this page.

Does the estimate match the truth?

measured Each dot is one of the 856 pairs: true Jaccard against the fraction of the 112 MinHash values that agree. The band is ±2 standard deviations of a binomial estimate, 2√(J(1−J)/112). datatrove computes (shingles * a + b) % _mersenne_prime in unsigned 64-bit arithmetic (minhash.py:182), so the product wraps around before the modulus and the functions are not exactly the textbook universal hash; the dots show it does not matter in practice.

Bands and rows over the measured pairs

Choosing b and r is taught on Deduplication, section 3, whose Band designer draws 1 − (1 − sr)b for any setting and checks it against these same measured pairs (the first b×r of the 112 values split into consecutive bands, as datatrove's np.split does at minhash.py:187). The point to carry here: the curve is steepest near (1/b)1/r, 0.72 for FineWeb's 14 × 8, so pairs a little below a 0.75 target still become candidates and pairs just above it are sometimes missed.

Settings that need more hashes, measured on the same pairs

measured Signatures with 286 and 9,000 hash functions computed with datatrove's code (same shingles, same permutation generator, seed 1) for the 397 documents that appear in the 856 pairs; every other pair has Jaccard below 0.05, where these settings give a candidate probability below 10−12. Settings: published Dolma 3 pool README (allenai/dolma3 at 1a9daced, read 2026-10-14): web text used 26 bands of 11 (286 hashes) and then kept only pairs whose true Jaccard is at least 0.8; the same README says its PDF data used "the same parameters as FineWeb ... 14 bands of size 5", which is not FineWeb's 14 of 8. RefinedWeb (Penedo et al. 2023) used 9,000 hashes; its text says "20 buckets of 450", and only 450 bands of 20 rows reproduce its own published probabilities (76% at 0.75, 99.4% at 0.8). Read as written, 20 bands of 450 rows matches only byte-identical shingle sets: on our pairs it finds the 143 pairs with Jaccard 1 and nothing else.

Pairs on the decision boundary, labelled by hand

A seeded sample of 35 pairs with Jaccard between 0.4 and 1, each document used at most once (so the 25-document banner cluster cannot fill the sample), read and labelled: Bboth are boilerplate or an extraction failure, Sthe same text copied, Ta template page where only the item differs, Ddifferent main content sharing boilerplate. "Removed" says which of the two run0 dropped.

What the labels say
FineWeb's 14 × 8 rarely pairs two different documents directly; the one D pair it does (0.65) is two shops' pages dominated by the same terms-of-service template. The larger risk is chaining: clusters are connected components (union-find in MinhashDedupCluster, minhash.py:537-556), so a page with two sentences of real text joins the banner cluster through intermediate banner pages and is dropped, although its own pairs with its D partner were never candidates. Dolma 3 adds a check of the true Jaccard similarity (0.8) between documents inside each cluster, which can break such chains.

The 31 clusters MinHash found

Every cluster run0's MinHash step formed in our file, with what its members are (read by hand), its size and the spread of true Jaccard similarity inside it. Only hostnames are shown, never page text, except in the animation above.

measured Kinds: Bboilerplate or extraction failure, Sthe same text copied across sites, Ttemplate pages whose item differs, Mone page reached through two or more URLs (query strings, session ids: URL dedup cannot see these), Ddifferent content sharing a long template. None of the 31 is the same news article syndicated to two sites; inside one WARC file (1 of the crawl’s 90,000) such copies are rare, while FineWeb's per-crawl dedup sees all 90,000 files.

Exact substrings with suffix arrays

The problem. MinHash judges whole documents. A 600-byte disclaimer pasted into thousands of otherwise different pages leaves each page unique by Jaccard, but the model still reads the disclaimer thousands of times. The tool. A suffix array is the list of every starting position in a text, sorted by the text that follows each position. Identical spans then sit next to each other, so one pass over neighbours finds every span of length L or more that occurs twice anywhere. Lee et al. (2021) built this for C4 and the Pile; RefinedWeb and Dolma 3 used it after MinHash.

A suffix array of a tiny corpus, step by step

illustrative three short documents written for this demo, joined with a unique separator per document (#0, #1, ...) so no match can cross a boundary, as the real tool's loaders do with 0xFF 0xFF plus a document index. The array is built live in your browser. Real corpora use the same idea with a linear-time construction (the Rust tool), not this sort.

On the running example

measured Google's deduplicate-text-datasets (commit 4e9888ac, built here with Rust 1.99): make, then self-similar --length-threshold L and collect per threshold, on bytes (no tokenizer). Lee et al.'s 50-token threshold is about 230 bytes of English (GPT-2 averages about 4.6 characters per token on FineWeb); Dolma 3 used 500 bytes. Remove all is what the tool's ranges mean: self-similar writes every position of a repeated span, the first included (main.rs:900-922), so deleting the ranges deletes every copy. Keep one is what Dolma 3 says it added ("we ensure we keep at least one copy of each substring"); estimated here by keeping the first range of each distinct span. Building the array took about s for the MB extracted file; the array file is bytes per text byte (pointer width grows with the text: 5 or 6 bytes at hundreds of GB).

What it finds after MinHash
On the final stage, after MinHash, 0.86% of bytes still sit in spans of 100 bytes or more that occur twice; the longest are consent text, comment-form notices, returns policies and dealer price disclaimers, each on two pages whose remaining text differs, which MinHash cannot touch because the rest of each page differs:

Bloom filters: exact dedup in fixed memory

The problem. Exact dedup needs a set of every hash seen so far: billions of entries. The tool. A Bloom filter is an array of m bits and k hash functions. Adding an item sets the k bits its hashes point to; testing an item checks whether all k are set. A new item can find all its bits already set by others (a false positive: "seen" when it was not), but a seen item is never missed. The Dolma toolkit streams documents through one: for each paragraph, if the filter says "seen", mark it a duplicate, otherwise add it.

A 32-bit filter, one paragraph at a time

measured paragraphs: lines from the running example that recur on many sites (the table in the Exact section), fed in a fixed order with repeats. The hash functions here are FNV-1a with different seeds, computed live; Dolma uses k seeded ahash hashers (bloom_filter.rs:181-212). With 32 bits the filter fills fast and starts saying "seen" for new paragraphs: watch for red.

The formula and the real tool. After n distinct items, a fresh item collides with probability about (1 − e−kn/m)k, smallest at k = (m/n) ln 2. We ran the real Dolma toolkit (dolma 1.2.1, paragraph mode) on the 743,644 non-blank lines of the 19,241 extracted documents, whose exact count of repeats is 256,024 (487,620 distinct), with filters from 64 KiB to 64 MiB. Because a Bloom filter never misses a repeat, every mark beyond 256,024 is a false positive.

measured three runs per size (Dolma draws new random hash seeds for every filter, bloom_filter.rs:76-98, so false positives differ run to run); expected = the sum over the 487,620 new paragraphs of the formula at the filter's fill when each arrives (the filter fills as it streams), with Dolma's own choice of k = ⌈(m/n) ln 2⌉ (bloom_filter.rs:27-32). Measured and expected agree within about 1%. At 1 MiB (17 bits per distinct paragraph) 11 to 14 paragraphs of 487,620 are wrongly dropped; at 64 KiB a third of all new paragraphs would be.

Found in the source: --dedupe.min_words switches paragraph dedup off
In deduper.rs (lines 338-380) the word-count check is the first branch of an if / else if / else, and the deduplication sits in the final else, so whenever min_words is above 0 no paragraph ever reaches it. Measured: the same 64 MiB run with --dedupe.min_words 1 marks 0 paragraphs instead of 256,024. Document mode has the same branch structure (lines 261-277; read, not run). Two smaller notes: when no size is given, Dolma sizes the filter by doubling from 1 MiB until the formula meets the target rate (bloom_filter.rs:45-61), so small runs get at least 1 MiB; and datatrove's own Bloom filter caps its size with MAX_HASH = 1 << 32 - 1 (bloom_filter.py:20), which Python parses as 1 << 31.

Two other uses of the same structure: Dolma seeds a filter with benchmark test items and flags any training paragraph that hits it (decontamination); DCLM used a Bloom-filter variant for near duplicates, marking a document when most of its n-grams have been seen before, because it "scales more easily to datasets surpassing 10TB" than MinHash (published DCLM Section 4.3). datatrove ships a similar step, SingleBloomFilter: 13-word shingles, a document is a duplicate when more than 80% of them were seen (bloom_filter.py:39-42, 185).

Semantic dedup: neighbours in embedding space

The problem. Two pages can say the same thing in different words: no shared 5-word phrase, Jaccard near 0. The tool. Embed every document with a text encoder (a model that maps text to a vector so that similar meanings land close together), cluster the vectors with k-means, and inside each cluster drop a document whose cosine similarity to an earlier-ranked one is at least 1 − ε. That is SemDeDup (Abbas et al. 2023) as NeMo Curator 1.4.0 runs it on GPUs: rank each cluster with the documents farthest from the centroid first ("hard", its default), keep the first, and remove any later document too close to one before it (stages/deduplication/semantic/pairwise.py, docstring at lines 95-131; defaults embeddinggemma-300m, 100 clusters, ε = 0.01 in stages/text/deduplication/semantic.py:80-92).

measured on CPU: the 2,692 filtered documents embedded with the encoder inside the FineWeb-Edu classifier on disk (Snowflake arctic-embed-m, first 512 tokens, the [CLS] vector, normalised); about s on 4 threads. Dots: the 856 MinHash pairs (true Jaccard across, cosine up), plus the 30 most similar pairs that share almost no shingles (Jaccard below 0.3, drawn in the second colour). The dashed line is the cosine cut 1 − ε. k-means with 20 clusters removes almost the same documents as comparing all pairs (the counts below), because near-identical documents land in the same cluster.

What only semantic dedup finds here
The pairs on the left of the chart: cookie banners from different plugins (cosine 0.95 to 0.97, Jaccard under 0.05) and two casino-spam articles on different sites (cosine 0.97, Jaccard 0). Neither is worth training on, so here semantic dedup is doing a quality filter's job. At loose ε it starts removing documents no other method touches: at ε = 0.15 (k-means, 20 clusters) it removes ; read such removals before trusting a setting. On DCLM's benchmark, using SemDeDup as the selection step scored 27.1 Core against 27.5 for no model-based selection (published DCLM Table 4): as a selection method on its own it did not beat selecting nothing.

At larger scale: 50,000 FineWeb rows of the same crawl

Across files and across crawls: what per-crawl dedup leaves

FineWeb deduplicated each crawl on its own and found that deduplicating all 96 crawls against each other made the model worse (Deduplication, section 1, has the numbers; the Reading tab's section 4 says what they do and do not show). Two measurements on our file make the two scopes concrete.

1. Inside one crawl: what FineWeb's crawl-wide MinHash removed from our file

measured Joined on WARC-Record-ID with the 2,425 documents FineWeb kept from the same WARC file. Of our 2,692 filtered documents, the that we kept and FineWeb did not are where FineWeb's MinHash over all 90,000 files of CC-MAIN-2024-30 is the main suspect (other causes: FineWeb ran MinHash before its C4 and FineWeb rules, on a larger set, and its extraction differed on a few pages). Looking for their partners directly is a needle hunt: MinHash signatures of 50,000 random FineWeb rows from the rest of the crawl (0.02% of it) gave candidate pairs with our documents and inside the sample, as expected when each partner sits in one of 89,999 other files.

Being widened (disk budget raised on 2026-10-14): the same check against all 971,981 rows of FineWeb's parquet file 000_00000.parquet for this crawl (about 400 other WARC files), see src/dedup/dd_fwshard.py. Running at low priority on the shared machine (about 8 hours at the current load); this box fills in when it finishes.

2. Across crawls: the same URLs in older crawls

For every one of the 2,692 documents we looked its URL up in the URL index of four earlier crawls, fetched the capture, extracted it the same way and measured the true Jaccard similarity with our version. A pair at 0.8 or more would be removed by a global MinHash; per-crawl dedup keeps both.

measured URL index read from data.commoncrawl.org (cluster.idx, then one block of the sorted CDX index per lookup, the same lookup the index server performs), URLs in Common Crawl's SURT form; newest HTML capture with status 200; Trafilatura with run0's settings (5 s timeout); 5-word shingles as in datatrove.

What this shows, and what it does not
It does not show that removing those copies would hurt or help a model: FineWeb's ablation is the evidence for that, at its scale. It also counts only same-URL recaptures; the same text under a new URL (a syndicated article, a moved page) is extra duplication that a URL lookup cannot see.

What each method costs, scaled up

Set the corpus and the calculator estimates the memory or disk each method needs. Every formula is shown; defaults are one crawl's worth of documents reaching dedup in a FineWeb-style pipeline.

derived MinHash signatures: documents × hashes × 8 bytes (datatrove stores 64-bit values, plus a 4-byte document id per band, sorted per band on disk). Bloom filter: m/n = −ln p / (ln 2)2 bits per distinct item, one item per document here (paragraph dedup multiplies the item count by paragraphs per document: 39 per document in our extracted stage). Suffix array: text plus w bytes per text byte, w = ⌈log2(text bytes)/8⌉ (the tool's pointer width; 3 on our 8 MB final stage). Defaults: 109 documents and 3,200 bytes each (the mean of run0's 2,692 filtered documents is characters). Not shown: compute, which for MinHash is documents × shingles × hashes multiply-adds ( for our median document) and is embarrassingly parallel, and the shuffle that groups band values across machines.

Reading the source

The lines that decide behaviour, at the pinned versions used above. Paths are inside each repository.

datatrove 0.10.1, src/datatrove/pipeline/dedup/minhash.py (FineWeb's MinHash)
51-54 the defaults are FineWeb's setting: 
n_grams: int = 5
num_buckets: int = 14
hashes_per_bucket: int = 8
seed: int = 1
204-205 shingles are word 5-grams of simplify_text output (lowercase, punctuation removed, numbers normalised; utils/text.py:186-193), tokenised by a language-specific word tokenizer (spaCy for English, which is why the shared venv needs spaCy): 
for x in ngrams(
    self.word_tokenizer.word_tokenize(simplify_text(text, self.config.norm_config)),
182, 187 112 hash functions in one vectorised line, minimum per function, then split into 14 consecutive bands: 
phv = (shingles * a + b) % _mersenne_prime
for x in np.split(np.min(phv, axis=0).astype(...), self.config.num_buckets)
471 no pairwise comparison anywhere: each band's signatures are sorted on disk, merged with a heap, and only neighbours with equal band values are written as duplicate pairs: 
if last is not None and last.sig == v.sig:
537-556, 579 clusters are connected components (union-find with path compression and union by size), and every node that is not its cluster's root is removed: 
union_set[root_b] = root_a  # make the smallest one join the biggest one
...
if node != p:
There is no check of the true similarity, so a chain of candidates can join documents that are not similar to each other (the stove page above).
datatrove 0.10.1, sentence_dedup.py and bloom_filter.py
sentence_dedup.py 42-47 C4's rule as defaults: n_sentences = 3, min_doc_words = 50, min_num_sentences = 3. 96 self.hash_fc = create_hash_func(config.hash_config) reads the argument, not self.config: pass a config explicitly.
bloom_filter.py 39-40 duplicate_threshold: float = 0.8, n_grams: int = 13; 185 a document is a duplicate when duplicate_shingles / len(shingles) > duplicate_threshold. 20 MAX_HASH = 1 << 32 - 1 evaluates to 231.
Dolma toolkit 1.2.1 (Rust), src/bloom_filter.rs and src/deduper.rs
bloom_filter.rs 27-32 k = ⌈(m/n) ln 2⌉ from the configured size and estimated count; 34-43 the false-positive formula (1 − (1 − 1/m)kn)k; 45-61 without a size, start at 1 MiB and double until the formula meets the target; 76-98 seeds drawn from rand::thread_rng() (a new filter hashes differently every run); 214-235 insert and contains on 32-bit atomic words, shared by all threads without locks.

Google deduplicate-text-datasets (4e9888ac), src/main.rs
900 two neighbouring suffixes match when their first L bytes are equal: 
let does_match = suf2.len() >= length_threshold && suf1.len() >= length_threshold && suf1[..length_threshold] == suf2[..length_threshold];
914-922 every position of a run of matches is written, the first included, unless --only-save-one (which writes the span text instead of positions). So the standard pipeline removes every copy.
NeMo Curator 1.4.0, semantic dedup
stages/text/deduplication/semantic.py 80-92 defaults: model_identifier = "google/embeddinggemma-300m", n_clusters = 100, which_to_keep = "hard", eps = 0.01. stages/deduplication/semantic/pairwise.py 95-131 (docstring): within a ranked cluster, row i takes the maximum cosine with rows ranked before it, and is removed when that is at least 1 − ε; "an earlier candidate remains eligible here even if that candidate's own score later causes it to be removed". The pairwise kernel requires CUDA (line 141); the CPU version above re-implements the same rule in numpy.

Check yourself

Predict. On our 2,692 filtered documents, which kind of cluster is the biggest MinHash finds?
The banner: 25 documents from 25 sites whose extracted text is the same consent notice. Dedup is also an extraction check: big clusters of short documents usually mean the extractor kept boilerplate.
Predict. RefinedWeb's text says "20 buckets of 450" hashes. If you read that as 20 bands of 450 rows, which pairs become candidates?
Only identical sets: a band of 450 rows matches with probability s450, which is 10−44 at s = 0.8. Measured on our pairs: 143 candidates, all with Jaccard 1. 450 bands of 20 finds all 308 pairs at 0.8 or more.
Predict. On raw extracted text, suffix-array dedup at 100 bytes marks 17% of all bytes as repeated. If you keep one copy of each repeated span instead of deleting every copy, how much of that remains to remove?
Most repeated bytes are repeated many times, so the choice between "remove every copy" (the tool's default output) and "keep one" (Dolma 3) changes the result fourfold.

Common mistakes

Trusting cluster membership as similarity
MinHash clusters are connected components of candidate pairs; two members can be far apart. Check the true Jaccard of each member against the kept one (Dolma 3 checks at 0.8) or at least look at the largest clusters.
Copying band settings from prose
RefinedWeb's "20 buckets of 450" and Dolma 3's "the same parameters as FineWeb ... 14 bands of size 5" both disagree with the numbers they sit next to. Recompute the S-curve and check it reproduces the published probabilities.
Reading suffix-array output as "remove duplicates"
The ranges cover every copy. Deleting them deletes the text everywhere, including its first occurrence; decide whether you want that.
Setting an option without reading the branch it sits in
In Dolma 1.2.1, --dedupe.min_words turns deduplication off. Always run a tool on a sample where you know the right answer (here, an exact Python count) before running it on everything.
Measuring dedup on a single file and calling it the corpus rate
One WARC file shows 2.8% near-duplicates; FineWeb's per-crawl MinHash removed far more of the same file's documents, and across crawls more again. Duplication grows with the scope, and so does the cost.

Interview questions

How do you choose bands and rows for MinHash LSH?
Pick the similarity you care about, then b and r so the S-curve 1 − (1 − sr)b is steep there (threshold about (1/b)1/r); more rows make it sharper and lower recall, more bands raise recall and cost (signature size b×r). Then measure on labelled pairs from your data.
Exact, fuzzy, substring, semantic: when each?
Exact hashes first (cheap, removes the bulk at web scale: two thirds of Dolma 3's pool). MinHash for near-duplicate documents. Suffix arrays for boilerplate spans inside unique documents, with a minimum span length and a keep-one policy. Semantic dedup for paraphrase-level redundancy, mostly in synthetic or instruction data, and with a quality check because it removes real pages at loose thresholds.
Design dedup for a 100-crawl, 1010-document corpus.
Exact dedup by content hash first, sharded by hash. MinHash per crawl (or globally with counts kept, so mixing can decide repeats), signatures computed in parallel and grouped by band value with a shuffle, union-find on candidate pairs, a true-Jaccard check inside large clusters, keep the newest copy. Optional suffix-array pass per shard for boilerplate. Log what each step removes and sample it.
Why is a Bloom filter enough for exact dedup at scale?
Fixed memory (about 14 bits per item for 0.1% false positives), one streaming pass, no false negatives. The cost of a false positive is one unique item wrongly dropped, which at a rate of 10−3 is acceptable for paragraphs; measured here, 1 MiB for 487,620 distinct lines wrongly dropped 11 to 14.
Go deeper. The deduplication child page extends this lab. Related here: the Pipeline lab for the stages before dedup (extraction decides how much boilerplate dedup sees), the Quality lab for what a classifier keeps from the same documents, and Topic: rag-and-retrieval for embedding models, the machinery behind semantic dedup.

Sources: Lee et al., "Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better" (arXiv 2107.06499, 2021); Broder, "On the resemblance and containment of documents" (1997); Penedo et al., FineWeb (arXiv 2406.17557, 2024) and RefinedWeb (arXiv 2306.01116, 2023); Raffel et al., C4/T5 (arXiv 1910.10683); Abbas et al., SemDeDup (arXiv 2303.09540, 2023); Li et al., DCLM (arXiv 2406.11794, 2024); allenai/dolma3 pool README (commit 1a9daced, read 2026-10-14); code at the pinned commits named above. Scripts and outputs: src/dedup/.

Quality lab: which documents are worth training on, and who decides

Every modern web corpus runs a model that scores each document and keeps a top slice. This lab runs the two published scorers that define today's open corpora, the FineWeb-Edu classifier and the DCLM fastText classifier, plus CCNet's perplexity filter and a fastText classifier trained here, on the same documents: the 2,617 pages of our Common Crawl file that survived the Pipeline lab's heuristic filters and the Dedup lab's MinHash step (run0). Then it reads what they drop. Everything below was measured on an Apple M1 Pro (CPU, 4 threads, low priority on a shared machine) on 2026-10-14, except two runs on its GPU on 2026-10-15 that say so, unless it says published.

In one screen

  • The two classifiers that define today's open corpora mostly disagree. On our 2,617 documents the FineWeb-Edu classifier keeps and the DCLM classifier keeps at their published cut-offs; only are kept by both, an overlap of of the union. Nemotron-CC measured 10.1% on a whole crawl (published, Table 8). Their scores rank documents with a Spearman correlation of .
  • About a third of what both drop is fine text. Reading a stratified sample of 100 documents, about of the documents both classifiers drop would be worth training a general model on, and half of those were news. Neither reference set (school-level teaching material for one, instruction and Q&A data for the other) looks like news.
  • The cut-offs are not what they sound like. DCLM's "top 10%" is P(hq) ≥ (the lowest score in DCLM-baseline itself), so the classifier keeps documents it thinks are 98% likely not high quality; on already-filtered FineWeb that cut keeps of documents, not 10%.
  • One default changes the scores. datatrove's fastText filter joins lines with no space by default; the DCLM classifier then changes its keep decision on of our 2,617 documents.
  • Perplexity under a modern LM rewards generated text. Under Qwen3-0.6B the documents that read like machine-written SEO copy have median perplexity against for the rest (section 8).
  • A fastText classifier trained here in about two minutes on the FineWeb-Edu annotations reaches a binary F1 of against the LLM labels, where the published 110M-parameter encoder classifier reaches on the same rows.

What "quality" means here: three recipes

A quality filter is a model that gives each document a number, plus a rule that keeps documents above a cut-off. There is no definition of quality behind it other than what the model was trained to prefer, so the first question about any filter is: preferred over what, by whom?

The exact prompt Llama 3 graded with (FineWeb-Edu)

Verbatim from utils/prompt.txt in the classifier's repository (rev 284663cb), lines 1 to 14. Note the additive design: each point has its own criterion, and the fifth asks for "outstanding" material for primary or grade school. The FineWeb paper says this focus was chosen "to avoid having the LLM favor highly technical pages like arXiv abstracts".

Below is an extract from a web page. Evaluate whether the page has a high educational value and could be useful in an educational setting for teaching from primary school to grade school levels using the additive 5-point scoring system described below. Points are accumulated based on the satisfaction of each criterion: - Add 1 point if the extract provides some basic information relevant to educational topics, even if it includes some irrelevant or non-academic content like advertisements and promotional material. - Add another point if the extract addresses certain elements pertinent to education but does not align closely with educational standards. [...] - Award a third point if the extract is appropriate for educational use and introduces key concepts relevant to school curricula. [...] It may resemble an introductory section of a textbook or a basic tutorial [...] - Grant a fourth point if the extract highly relevant and beneficial for educational purposes for a level not higher than grade school [...] - Bestow a fifth point if the extract is outstanding in its educational value, perfectly suited for teaching either at primary school or grade school. [...] The extract: <EXAMPLE>. After examining the extract: - Briefly justify your total score, up to 100 words. - Conclude with the score using the format: "Educational score: <total points>"
Predict: DCLM-baseline "keeps the top 10%" of its pool by the classifier's probability that a page is high quality. What is the lowest probability among the documents it kept?
0.0181. The smallest fasttext_score among the first 50,000 rows of DCLM-baseline 1.0 is , and 10% of them score below (measured). The classifier was trained on balanced classes but the crawl is overwhelmingly unlike the positives, so almost every page gets a tiny probability and only the ranking matters. Read a fastText probability as a rank, never as a calibrated chance.

The same shard, before and after each filter

Click any square to open it in the inspector (section 5). The "either keeps" filter is a stand-in for Nemotron-CC's ensemble, which takes the maximum of its classifiers' bucket ranks; it is not their exact recipe (their classifiers and thresholds differ). Words are counted by splitting on whitespace.

Watch the pile, not the survivors. Run FineWeb-Edu, then switch to DCLM: different squares fall, and step 6 outlines how many of each filter's survivors the other would have thrown away. Switch to "both must keep" and the shard shrinks to documents; "either keeps" keeps . That gap is the whole argument of Nemotron-CC: classifiers with different targets find different good documents, so an ensemble keeps more good text at a given quality.

Do the two classifiers agree?

Two ways to ask it. Rank correlation (Spearman) asks whether they order all documents the same way. Top-slice overlap asks what a filter actually does: if each keeps its top k%, how much of what one keeps does the other keep? The overlap is shown as intersection over union, the measure Nemotron-CC's Table 8 reports.

10% each

Reading it. On our WARC, when each keeps its top 10% the overlap is of the union ( of either slice), against about 5% for two unrelated random filters; on 2,000 random FineWeb rows of the same crawl it is . At the published cut-offs the two keep very different amounts (FineWeb-Edu , DCLM of our documents), and the overlap is . Nemotron-CC's figure, 10.1% on CC-MAIN-2021-21, sits in the same range, measured on a whole crawl rather than one file. On the Nemotron-CC sample the correlation is higher ( against ) because those buckets span the whole quality range, including the very low end that both models agree on: agreement depends on the population, and the hard, disputed documents are the ones in the middle of an already filtered crawl.

Agreement at scale without the encoder: DCLM against the LLM grades themselves

Scoring 50,000 documents with the FineWeb-Edu encoder needed the GPU (done, section 8), but the DCLM classifier is cheap, so it was run on all 232,000 Llama 3 annotations the FineWeb-Edu classifier was trained from. The share passing DCLM's cut rises steadily with the LLM's educational score: the two notions of quality point the same way, weakly (Spearman ).

The first 4 of the 8 annotation files (232,000 pages from CC-MAIN-2024-10), DCLM P(hq) ≥ . Score 5 has only 6 pages here. On the 50,000-row FineWeb-Edu sample, of documents pass DCLM's cut ( on the 50,000-row FineWeb sample).

What the filters wrongly drop (and wrongly keep)

Method. The 2,617 documents were split into five strata by what the two classifiers do at their published cut-offs, and 20 documents were drawn from each (seed 0), so the rare disagreements get as many reads as the common case. Each was read (its first 900 characters) and labelled: would I want it in the pretraining data of a general language model? Yes means coherent, informative or well-formed natural text of any kind (news, how-to, recipes, reviews, essays, organisation pages with real content); no means commerce boilerplate, navigation, cookie banners, templated directory pages, spun or keyword-stuffed text; unsure otherwise. A second tag records the format and whether the text reads like spun or machine-generated SEO copy.

Who labelled. The agent that built this lab (Claude), on 2026-10-14; the labels, with a one-line reason each, are committed in src/qual/labels.jsonl (ids only, no text) so they can be re-labelled by a person. One labeller and 20 documents per stratum: each stratum's share has a 95% interval of roughly ±20 points. And human judgement is not the target: DCLM had 16 annotators label about 500 pages (71% inter-annotator agreement) and found that a filter's agreement with them did not predict how good a model trained on its output was (AskLLM agreed best, about 82% ROC-AUC, and trained worse models than fastText filters at about 73%; DCLM, Appendix on human judgement). So "wrongly dropped" below means "dropped although a reader would call it fine text", not "proven to hurt".

Hand labels by stratum: worth training on / unsure / not

worth training onunsurenot worth it
  • Wrong drops. Weighting each stratum by its size, about of what the FineWeb-Edu cut drops and of what the DCLM cut drops is text labelled worth training on; among documents both drop it is .
  • The over-represented format is news. Of the documents both classifiers drop that were labelled worth keeping, are news reports or press releases. Neither reference resembles news: FineWeb-Edu's prompt asks for primary and grade-school teaching value, DCLM's positives are instructions and explanatory answers. Other wrong drops: organisation pages with real content, personal blogs, a recipe, a book review.
  • Wrong keeps belong to DCLM. of the 20 documents only DCLM keeps were labelled not worth it: a cookie-consent table (P(hq) 0.88), a personal site's navigation stub (0.84), a templated location page, a keyword-stuffed sales post, a two-sentence product description. A bag-of-bigrams model reacts to phrasing ("Please keep in mind", "This cookie is used to") without reading the page. No document that FineWeb-Edu keeps was labelled not worth it.
  • A bias worth checking at scale. of the 20 documents both keep read like machine-generated SEO explainers ("In this article, we will dive into..."), against spun pages among the 20 lowest. Both classifiers reward fluent, explanatory prose, which is exactly what LLM-written filler is. This is the labeller's impression, not a measurement; a detector run would be the test.

Train your own quality classifier (on a laptop CPU)

The FineWeb-Edu recipe has two expensive parts: the LLM grades (460,000 Llama-3-70B calls) and the encoder that imitates them. The grades are public, so the second part can be redone with something much cheaper. Here a fastText classifier, the same kind as DCLM's, learns the binary question "did Llama 3 give this page 3 or more?" from of the published annotations, and is tested on it never saw.

How fastText classifies, from its source (fastText v0.9.2): the text is split on whitespace (src/dictionary.cc:208-232; a newline becomes an end-of-sentence token), each word and each word pair is hashed into one of 2 million rows of an embedding table (dictionary.cc:312-323: h = h * 116049371 + hashes[j], then h % bucket), the document vector is the average of its rows (src/model.cc:42-50), and one linear layer with a softmax gives the label probabilities. No attention, no word order beyond pairs: that is why it scores a document in about 2 ms on one core and why it can be fooled by phrasing.

Our fastText: F1 against how many annotations it trained on

F1 of the "score ≥ 3" class on held-out annotations; dots are seeds (3 seeds up to 20,000 examples, 1 above), the line their mean; threshold on P(hq) chosen on a separate validation split each time. Dashed: the published FineWeb-Edu classifier's F1 on 1,500 of the same held-out rows (see the caveat below). Config chosen on validation: .

Binary F1 (score ≥ 3)Macro F1 (both classes)Spearman with the Llama 3 scoreSize, speed
Published FineWeb-Edu classifier (encoder + linear head)438 MB; 0.14 s per document on 4 CPU threads
Our fastText (bigrams), same 1,500 rows; about 2 minutes to train on 4 threads

On all held-out rows our classifier's F1 is (precision , recall , threshold P(hq) ≥ ). Caveat on the published model's row: the 1,500 rows come from the classifier's own training data. Its train/test split cannot be rebuilt (the card's hold-out of 46,867 rows implies about 468,670 annotations at training time; the dataset now holds 467,424), so roughly 90% of these rows were seen in training. With a frozen encoder and a single linear output (769 trainable numbers fitted on 410,000 examples) memorisation is negligible, and its six-class accuracy here, , is close to the card's 71% on its true hold-out.

What "F1 82%" means. The FineWeb paper and the card both report "an F1 score of 82%" at threshold 3, without saying which F1. On the 1,500 rows the published classifier's F1 for the positive class is and the macro F1 over the two classes is ; the training script selects checkpoints by six-class macro F1 (train_edu_bert.py:31, 91), which is here and 50% on the card's hold-out. The 82% is most consistent with the two-class macro F1. Always ask which F1, on which class balance: 9% of pages are positives, so a classifier that drops everything has 91% accuracy.

So is an encoder worth it? On the same rows the encoder beats bigrams clearly in F1 and rank correlation, and takes about 60 times longer per document (0.14 s on 4 threads against about 2 ms on one). On our 2,617 documents our fastText ranks like the published classifier with a Spearman of (and with DCLM's), and keeps documents at its threshold. This is the trade every pipeline makes: DCLM chose fastText for the whole 240T-token pool; FineWeb-Edu paid 6,000 H100 hours for the encoder.

Nemotron-CC: keep more, sorted into buckets

Nemotron-CC scores every document with three classifiers (two FineWeb-Edu-style encoders trained on Mistral 8x22B and Nemotron-340B grades, plus DCLM's fastText), turns each classifier's ranking into 20 buckets of about 5% each, takes the maximum bucket over the three, and groups the 20 buckets into 5 quality levels by annealing an 8B model on each (published, Section 2.2). The public data is partitioned by those levels, so the first 200 documents of each level for CC-MAIN-2024-30 were scored here with the two public classifiers.

Share passing DCLM's cut, by Nemotron-CC level

Share passing FineWeb-Edu's cut, by level

Both scores fall monotonically from high to low, which checks that the buckets mean what the paper says. Two things stand out. DCLM passes of "high" and of "medium-high" but only of "medium": the DCLM cut sits near Nemotron's top two levels. FineWeb-Edu passes only of "high": with a maximum over three classifiers, most of Nemotron's top level is there because DCLM or the other classifiers liked it, not the educational one. These are head samples of one part file per level, not a random sample of the levels.

Why not join Nemotron-CC to our WARC? Its files are partitioned by quality level, not by source WARC; finding our file's documents would mean scanning all 722 part files of CC-MAIN-2024-30 (see the root's data README). Nemotron-CC did not use the FineWeb-Edu classifier itself "for license issue, since it is trained with annotations from Llama3" (footnote 18).

Perplexity filtering, CCNet's way

CCNet tokenises each page with SentencePiece, scores it with a 5-gram KenLM model trained on that language's Wikipedia, and computes the page's perplexity: 10 to the power of minus the average log10 probability per token, so a page the model finds predictable gets a low number. Pages are then split by per-language cut-offs into head, middle and tail. Its original English models were downloaded (4.4 GB) and its code ported line for line; the probe sentences from the model's documentation come out at 685 ("I am very perplexed") and 12,223 ("im hella trippin"), the same direction as documented.

CCNet perplexity of our 2,617 documents

Green: head (below 340, the 30th percentile of English in cc_net's cutoff.csv); yellow: middle (340 to 520, the 60th percentile); grey: tail. Measured: head , middle , tail ; median . Single CPU thread, under 3 minutes for all documents (measured, rough).

Perplexity measures "looks like Wikipedia", which overlaps with quality only partly: it ranks our documents with Spearman against the FineWeb-Edu score and against DCLM. Of the head bucket, FineWeb-Edu keeps and DCLM ; of the tail, and . The paper itself warns that "Some documents despite being valid text ends up in the tail because they have a vocabulary very different from Wikipedia" (Section 5). One more thing from the code: the paper says each language is split into "three even parts", while PerplexityBucket uses the 30th and 60th percentiles (cc_net/perplexity.py:257-286), so head is 30% and tail 40% of the reference crawl.

The same idea with a modern small LM (run on the GPU queue, 2026-10-15)

CCNet's 5-gram model knows only Wikipedia. The same 2,617 documents were also scored by Qwen3-0.6B, a 0.6B-parameter LM trained on web-scale data: perplexity of the first 512 tokens (float16 weights on the M1 Pro GPU, log-softmax in float32; q_ppl.py). Median perplexity . Its ranking agrees with CCNet's only moderately (Spearman ; the two "lowest 30%" sets overlap of their union), and with the quality classifiers weakly: Spearman with the FineWeb-Edu score and with DCLM's. FineWeb-Edu keeps of Qwen3's least-surprising 30% and of its most-surprising 30%; DCLM keeps and . So a lower-perplexity third is a better third by both classifiers, weakly. The striking part is at the bottom of the scale: the 12 least surprising documents (perplexity ) all read like machine-generated SEO explainers ("Are you in need of large custom aluminum extrusions for your next project?"), and among the 60 hand-labelled documents that at least one classifier keeps, the flagged as reading like generated text (flagged while labelling, a day before this run) have median perplexity against for the other (CCNet: against ). In this sample a modern LM finds generated-looking text the least surprising, so a "keep low perplexity" rule with such a reference model would favour generated filler. The filter's meaning lives in its reference model, exactly as with the classifiers.

The agreement study at 25 times the size (GPU queue)

The FineWeb-Edu classifier was run on all 50,000 rows of the FineWeb CC-MAIN-2024-30 sample (the same 50,000 rows the Dedup lab uses), next to the DCLM scores already computed on CPU; on the 2,000 rows also scored on CPU the GPU scores agree to within 0.00001. FineWeb-Edu's cut keeps of documents ( of tokens), DCLM's ; documents pass both, an overlap of of the union; with each keeping its top 10% the overlap is , and the rank correlation is . These match the 2,617-document and 2,000-document measurements above, so the disagreement is not an artefact of a small sample.

Traps found while reproducing

  1. Newlines change DCLM's scores. fastText's Python predict refuses text containing "\n" (FastText.py:211-213), so every pipeline must flatten lines first. DCLM and the Dolma toolkit join lines with a space (dolma/taggers/quality.py:29); datatrove's FastTextClassifierFilter replaces "\n" with newline_replacement, whose default is the empty string (datatrove/pipeline/filters/fasttext_filter.py:47, 99), gluing the last word of one line to the first of the next. With the space, our scores reproduce DCLM-baseline's stored fasttext_score to within on 2,000 rows; with datatrove's default they differ by 0.07 on average and up to 0.97, and on our WARC the keep decision flips for of 2,617 documents. Pass newline_replacement=" ".
  2. "Top 10%" is a pool-relative threshold. DCLM's cut, P(hq) ≥ 0.0181, was the 90th percentile of DCLM-Pool after RefinedWeb-style filters. Applied to other data it keeps whatever fraction lands above it: of our documents, of FineWeb, of FineWeb-Edu. To reproduce a keep fraction, recompute the percentile on your own pool.
  3. Three different dataset sizes for one classifier. The FineWeb paper says 460,000 annotations with 410,000 for training and 50,000 held out; the card says it was trained on 450,000 and evaluated on a hold-out of 46,867; the annotation dataset today has 467,424 rows (8 files of 58,428). None of these is wrong on its own terms, but the published split cannot be rebuilt.
  4. F1 without a definition (section 6), and rounding: int_score is int(round(max(0, min(score, 5)))) (run_edu_bert.py:24), so "int_score ≥ 3" means score above 2.5; NeMo Curator labels a document high quality when the raw score is ≥ 2.5 (nemo_curator/stages/text/classifiers/fineweb_edu.py:117-118). Python rounds 2.5 down to 2, so the two differ only at exactly 2.5.
  5. The published scores do reproduce on CPU. On FineWeb-Edu's 159 rows from our WARC, our float32 CPU scores differ from the stored ones by at most 0.024 (the published run used bfloat16 on GPU, run_edu_bert.py:9), and 158 of 159 rounded scores match. All FineWeb-Edu documents that are also in run0's output score ≥ 2.5 here (), and only of our other documents do: our extraction, filters and scores reproduce theirs almost exactly on this file.
  6. One fastText config diverged. Unigrams with learning rate 0.1 stopped with "Encountered NaN" on the full 188k-row training file, while bigram configs trained fine; on a 20,000-row subset the same config trains. Lower the learning rate or check for extremely long lines (the longest training document has about 37,000 tokens) before concluding a feature set is worse.
