Common mistakes, and interview questions

  • Reading a classifier probability as a calibrated chance. DCLM keeps pages it rates 2% likely to be "high quality". Thresholds are percentiles of a pool.
  • Copying a threshold across datasets. A cut that keeps 10% of a raw pool keeps 25% of FineWeb and 61% of FineWeb-Edu.
  • Trusting a library default for preprocessing. One empty-string default flips 4% of keep decisions here.
  • Judging a filter by its agreement with people. DCLM found no correlation between agreement with human labels and the trained model's quality. Judge filters by training small models on their output.
  • Forgetting what the reference excludes. An educational filter removes news and fiction by design; a filter trained on instructions rewards text that sounds like an answer, including generated filler and cookie banners.
  • Scoring only the start of a document. The encoder sees 512 tokens; a long page is judged on its opening.
Interview questions with short answers

Why use a fastText classifier at all when encoders are better? Cost at the scale that matters: a few milliseconds per document on one CPU core against a GPU forward pass; DCLM scored a 240T-token pool. Here the encoder agreed better with the LLM labels (F1 against ) at about 60 times the time per document, on 4 threads against one.

Your quality filter keeps 10%. Your run needs 15T tokens and you have 1.3T after filtering. What do you do? Repeat (up to about 4 epochs costs little, Muennighoff et al.), loosen the threshold, ensemble classifiers with different targets to raise recall (Nemotron-CC), and rephrase the lower tiers with an LLM instead of dropping them; check each choice with small annealing runs.

How do you know a quality filter is not throwing away something important? Stratified sample of what it drops, read and labelled; per-domain and per-format drop rates; perplexity of the trained model on held-out slices such as news, dialects and code; and ablation models trained with and without the filter.

Two classifiers keep 10% each and overlap 15%. Which do you use? Neither choice is answered by the overlap; train small models on each kept set and on the union, and compare on your target evaluations. Low overlap says the union is a cheap way to more good tokens.

What does the LLM-annotation step cost, and what is it for? Hundreds of thousands of LLM calls once (FineWeb-Edu: 460,000 pages); the labels then train a small model that is cheap enough for the whole crawl. The prompt is the real definition of quality, so read it.

Published numbers: FineWeb (arXiv 2406.17557), DCLM (arXiv 2406.11794), Nemotron-CC (arXiv 2412.02595), Tables 8 and 9, CCNet (arXiv 1911.00359), FineWeb-Edu classifier card, DCLM fastText model, all read 2026-10-14. Measured inputs: the root's running example (src/data/README.md), FineWeb-Edu Llama 3 annotations rev 72df4c92, Nemotron-CC head samples, cc_net's English LM. The sibling child page on quality classifiers and data selection will go deeper.

A pretraining run draws its tokens from several domains (web, code, math, papers, encyclopedias, ...) and the mixture says how many tokens come from each, and when. This lab gives the overview: what the weights mean, how temperature sampling and repetition trade off on the running example's real domain sizes, how labs choose weights with small proxy models, how a short final stage changes the same token budget, and why aggressive filtering makes long runs a mixing problem.

Labels: measured here on an Apple M1 Pro (CPU) on 2026-10-14 or 15; published by the authors at their scale, not rerun here; derived by a stated formula from published or measured numbers. The depth (a DoReMi step-by-step animation, a mixing-law fitter on RegMix's 1,088 released runs, a stage-by-stage token-budget planner) is on the child page Data mixing, curricula and continued-pretraining ratios.

From zeroCalculatorChoosing weightsProxy experimentStagingLong horizonsCPT ratioCheck yourself

From zero: domains, weights, budgets, epochs

Domain
A source of text with its own character: filtered web pages, source code, math pages, scientific papers, an encyclopedia. Each comes as a pool of unique tokens (after filtering and dedup).
Token budget
How many tokens the run trains on in total, fixed in advance by the compute you have (the training topic's scaling section explains how).
Mixture weight
The share of the budget drawn from a domain. Weights sum to 1. At a fixed budget a point of code is a point not spent on web text, so the weights move abilities directly.
Natural share
A domain's size divided by the total: what you get by concatenating everything and shuffling. Small, valuable domains get almost nothing.
Epoch
One pass over a domain's unique tokens. Weight times budget divided by pool size = epochs of that domain. More than 1 means repetition (upsampling); less than 1 means part of the pool is never seen.
Temperature sampling
Weight each domain by its size raised to the power 1/T, then normalise. T = 1 is the natural share, larger T flattens toward uniform. Multilingual models use it to give small languages more: mBERT used 1.43, XLM 2, XLM-R and mT5 3.33 (as tabulated in UniMax, Table 1).

The running example's five domains, at their real sizes

The proxy experiment below (shared with the child page) trains on five domains, each a public dataset the topic's samples come from. Their full sizes are published in five different units, because each card counts with its own tokenizer, or in words or bytes. Converting them to one unit is the first step of any mixing plan; here each is converted to GPT-2 tokens with a ratio measured on the topic's sample of that dataset.

Mixture calculator: temperature, epochs and what repetition is worth

Pick a token budget and a way to set the weights. The calculator shows each domain's weight, the tokens it supplies, its epochs, and its fresh-token equivalent: Muennighoff et al. fit how much repeated data is worth, D′ = U + U·R*·(1 − e−R/R*), with U unique tokens, R repetitions beyond the first pass and R* = 15.39 fitted (arXiv 2305.16264, App. A, published). Four epochs are worth 3.73 fresh passes (93%), sixteen are worth 10.58 (66%), and no amount of repetition is worth more than about 16.4 passes. The law was fitted on one corpus at a time; applying it per domain is this calculator's approximation (derived).

UniMax (arXiv 2304.09151, Algorithm 1): smallest domain first, each gets an equal share of what is left, but never more than N epochs; the rest flows to the larger domains.

Bars: top, natural shares (T = 1); bottom, your setting, sliding from the natural shares when you change it. Epochs in orange pass 4 (the point after which Muennighoff et al. see measurable loss), underlined past 16 (repetition is then worth little). The curve is the value of a repeated token (D′ divided by tokens drawn) against epochs; the dots are your domains. Sizes are GPT-2 tokens, converted as in the table above.

Predict: at a 4T budget, how many epochs of English Wikipedia does temperature T = 3.33 (the mT5 setting) ask for?
What the calculator teaches
Natural shares starve every small domain; temperature fixes that but knows nothing about repetition, so at a large budget it repeats a small domain dozens of times, where each extra pass is worth little. UniMax was designed for exactly this: it caps epochs and spends the rest on the large pools. Which domain deserves more is a separate question that sizes cannot answer; that is what the proxy methods below measure.

Choosing weights without paying for the big run

Sizes say how much of each domain exists, not how much it helps. Every published method answers the second question the same way: train proxy models (small models, cheap runs) on different mixtures, measure, and transfer the answer to the big run. They differ in what they train and how they read the answer.

MethodWhat it trainsHow it picks the weightsReported result (published)
Heuristicsnothingnatural, temperature, UniMax, or a mix that worked beforeStill the baseline every method is compared with; a published mix was tuned for someone else's model size and budget.
DoReMia 280M reference model, then a 280M proxyGroup DRO: during proxy training, upweight the domains whose loss is furthest above the reference's (the excess loss); average the weights over trainingAn 8B model on the weights gained 6.5 points average one-shot accuracy and reached the baseline's accuracy 2.6 times faster; the search cost 8% of the 8B run's compute (DoReMi).
Data Mixing Lawsmany small runs at different mixturesfit loss as c + k·exp(Σ tjrj) of the proportions r, nest it with scaling laws, minimiseA 1B model on 100B RedPajama tokens matched the default mix trained 48% longer (arXiv 2403.16952).
RegMix512 models of 1M parameters, 1B tokens each, random mixturesregress loss on the mixture (linear or LightGBM), score many candidate mixtures, average the bestBeat DoReMi on the 1B check below at about a tenth of its search compute (RegMix).
The check: Aiolire-runs of the methods on the same data(a new method, plus a test of the others)No existing method beat simple stratified sampling (equal weight per domain) on average test perplexity in every setting (Aioli, Table 2, third-party for the methods it tests).

One table, six mixtures: RegMix's 1B-parameter check

RegMix trained a 1B model on 25B tokens of The Pile with each mixture and averaged 14 downstream tasks. The differences are a point or two of average accuracy, and the simplest alternative, web text only, ties DoReMi.

RegMix, Table 4, published; values as transcribed on the child page. "Best on" counts the 14 tasks where a mixture scored highest. The axis starts at 44, not 0. Search compute in FLOPs: DoReMi 3.7e19, RegMix 3.5e18 (); Human, ODM and Pile-CC need no search.

Correction kept from the child page
DoReMi's "baseline" and RegMix's "Human" are not The Pile's own Table 1 weights: they are a document-count weighting from DoReMi's repository (Wikipedia 9.19% against 1.53% in The Pile's Table 1). So "+6.5 points over The Pile's default weights" really means over that weighting. The child page compares the two weightings domain by domain.

The running example's own proxy experiment

The child page designed one small experiment on the five domains above, so the page can show a mixture regression fitted on its own data rather than only quoting papers. This tab reuses it unchanged (no second experiment): the same script, the same pools, the same outputs.

PartDesign
Data20M to 42M GPT-2 training tokens per domain streamed from the five datasets above (same files and revisions as the topic's samples), about 5% held out per domain. The experiment's "natural" shares are those pool sizes (15% to 31%), not the real-world shares of the table above (web ).
Proxy modelA tiny GPT: 793,344 parameters outside the embedding (7,259,008 with the tied 50,257-token embedding), context 256.
SweepDesigned, not run (dropped 2026-10-15): 48 mixtures drawn as in RegMix (a Dirichlet whose parameters are the pool shares times a scale drawn between 0.1 and 5, so some mixtures are near-uniform and some almost one domain), 2,000 steps of 32 × 256 tokens (16.4M tokens) each; plus three anchors: natural, uniform, temperature 2.
Target and fitDesigned, not run: mean held-out loss over the five domains (one choice among several: RegMix targeted Pile-CC validation loss); the Data Mixing Laws form fitted to the sweep; then RegMix's selection: score 100,000 sampled mixtures, average the best 128.
DoReMiRun on 2026-10-16: a reference proxy on natural shares, then Group DRO (η = 1), 4,000 steps of 30 × 256 tokens each, M1 Pro GPU.
Rank checkDesigned, not run: two larger models (10.6M non-embedding) on about 98M tokens each: natural shares against the predicted best. If the best still wins at this scale, the regression transferred.

Staging: the same token budget before and after a mid-training stage

Modern runs change the mixture during training: a long first stage on broad data, then a short final stage on the best data (math, instruction-like and question-answer text, filtered web, often partly synthetic) while the learning rate decays to zero. Labs call it mid-training or annealing. The animation takes OLMo 2 7B's real budget, 4T tokens of pretraining plus 50B tokens of the Dolmino mix, and plays it two ways: the published two stages, and one static mixture containing the same tokens per group spread evenly over the run.

OLMo 2, Tables 4, 9 and 13, published. Stage 1 is drawn with the shares of the 3.90T-token OLMo 2 1124 Mix (Table 4; the 7B trained 4T tokens on it); stage 2 with the 50B Dolmino mix's "Mix %" column (Table 13). Groups are this page's: arXiv counts as papers, FLAN and Stack Exchange as instruction and Q&A, the filtered DCLM slice of stage 2 as high-quality web. Token counts per group are derived as share times stage tokens. The learning-rate line is a sketch of the published schedule (warmup, cosine decay toward 10% of the peak, then linear decay to zero during mid-training), not a plot of logged values. What the stage bought (GSM8K 24.1 to 67.5) is on the Reading tab, section 7.

How big is the final stage? It depends on the lab

published stage sizes, fraction of the run's tokens derived; log scale. Not a rule: from 40 million tokens to 40% of the run. OLMo 2's own text calls mid-training "5 to 10% of training FLOPs" because it counts every mid-training run averaged into the final model ("souping"): three runs of 50B for the 7B (), three of 100B and one of 300B for the 13B (). Any single path to the final 7B weights saw 50B mid-training tokens, 1.2% of its tokens. Llama 3 also has a long-context stage of about 800B tokens before its annealing.

Go deeper. The child page's Token-budget planner tab lets you set your own pools, stages and weights and plays the same tokens in both orders, with presets for SmolLM2, SmolLM3 and OLMo 2.

Long horizons: where mixing meets dedup and quality filtering

The quality lab's classifiers keep the top slice of the web; dedup removes copies. Both shrink the pool of unique tokens, and a long run must then repeat it. Nemotron-CC made this argument with numbers: DCLM-baseline and FineWeb-Edu "contain around 80% near-duplicates", leaving about 1T and 0.2T unique tokens, while their filters remove 90% of the data; a 15T-token run (Llama 3.1's horizon) on either would see the same documents many times (Nemotron-CC, Section 1 and Table 4). Its answer was to keep more of the crawl (an ensemble of classifiers sorted into quality buckets instead of one cut) and to add rephrased synthetic text.

Dataset sizes and unique tokens (after global fuzzy dedup of the real tokens): Nemotron-CC, Table 4, published, trillions of tokens. Epochs and fresh-token equivalents are derived: the whole budget drawn from one corpus's unique tokens, valued with Muennighoff et al.'s law as in the calculator. Nemotron-CC's 1.9T synthetic tokens are left out of "unique"; counting them as fresh would raise its bar further. A thought experiment, not a training result.

What the labs did with it
Nemotron-CC's own 15T run was staged: a first phase of 9T tokens with 59% English Common Crawl (5.31T, the medium, medium-high and high buckets, real and synthetic) and a second phase of 6T with 31% (1.86T, high quality only), 7.17T in total; the 8B model scored MMLU 70.3 against 65.3 for Llama 3.1 8B in NVIDIA's own evaluation setup (Appendix E and Table 6, published). In a 1T-token ablation, swapping 4 of 8 epochs of the high-quality data for synthetic rephrasings improved most benchmarks (Section 3). So the quality tiers are mixing domains in their own right: the top tier is repeated, the middle tiers supply unique tokens, and synthetic data replaces repetitions.

Continued pretraining: how much domain data before the model forgets

Continued pretraining (CPT) is the same mixing decision made later: train a finished model further on one domain and mix general data back in (replay) or it forgets. The CMR scaling law reads the critical mixture ratio, the largest share of domain data that keeps general loss within a tolerance, off a few short probe runs; bigger models and domains closer to the general data tolerate more (29.8% to 47.8% on finance from 460M to 3.1B, Gu et al., arXiv 2407.17467). Data mixing, section 6, owns CPT: forgetting, re-warming, schedules and a CMR calculator with these ratios; this lab's bar chart of them was retired on 2026-10-24.

Check yourself

Predict: OLMo 2 7B's mid-training is 1.2% of its tokens. What share of all the math tokens the model saw came in that stage?
Predict: in RegMix's 1B check, how did training on web text only (Pile-CC) compare with DoReMi's optimised mixture?
The same average, 46.8 against 46.8, and web-only was best on 5 of the 14 tasks against none for DoReMi. RegMix's mixture (47.3) put 87% on Pile-CC. Web text is broad; much of what a mixture search finds is "more web".

Common mistakes

Mixing sizes counted with different tokenizers
Cards count tokens with their own tokenizer, or in words or bytes. Code is where it bites: on the topic's Stack v2 Edu sample GPT-2 needs tokens for every Comma v0.1 token. Convert everything to your tokenizer on a sample before computing epochs.
Temperature sampling at a large budget without counting epochs
Temperature knows sizes, not repetition. At 15T with T = 3.33, English Wikipedia would be repeated times. Cap epochs (UniMax) or accept that the extra passes are worth little.
Copying a published mixture
Optimal weights shift with model size and budget, and DoReMi's weights from the paper's 280M proxy and from its repository's 120M proxy differ widely on the same data (Pile-CC 60.6% against 13.8%, compared on the child page). Treat a published mix as a starting point and re-run a cheap search on your own pools.
Calling the late stage "the final 10 to 30%"
OLMo 2 7B's mid-training is about 1.2% of its tokens, SmolLM2's decay stage 9%, Llama 3's annealing 40M tokens; Nemotron-CC's high-quality phase is 40%. There is no standard size; the common element is a different, higher-quality mix while the learning rate decays.
Reading DoReMi's or RegMix's gains as gains over The Pile's weights
Their baseline is a document-count weighting from DoReMi's repository, not The Pile's Table 1. The gains are real but measured against that baseline.

Interview questions

You have 3T unique web tokens, 50B code, 20B math and a 10T-token budget. How do you set the mix?
Convert all pools to the training tokenizer. Start from capped epochs: code and math at no more than about 4 epochs over the run (200B and 80B), the rest web (about 3.2 passes over 3T, so even web repeats). Put most of the math and code repetitions in a final decay stage. Check with a cheap proxy search (RegMix-style small models, or an annealing test per source) and confirm the chosen mix against natural and stratified baselines; expect differences of a point or two.
Why does aggressive quality filtering become a problem at 15T tokens?
It shrinks the unique pool (FineWeb-Edu about 0.2T unique, DCLM about 1T by Nemotron-CC's estimate), so a long run repeats it 15 to 75 times, far past the 4-epoch point where repetition starts to cost. Keep lower tiers for unique tokens, repeat the top tier a few times, add rephrased data, and stage it.
How would you test whether a new 10B-token dataset is worth adding?
An annealing test: take a mid-run checkpoint, decay the learning rate over a short run with the candidate at a fixed share (Llama 3 used 30% of 40B tokens), compare with the same run without it. Cheaper than retraining and sensitive to small, high-quality sources; OLMo 2 ran 19 such "microanneals" for 130B tokens in total.
DoReMi or RegMix: which would you run, and what would you check?
RegMix if many tiny runs are cheap to parallelise (it found its mix with about a tenth of DoReMi's search compute); DoReMi if you can afford two mid-size runs and want weights tied to excess loss. Either way check transfer: rank a few mixtures at the small scale, then train two of them at a larger scale and see if the order holds (the proxy experiment's rank check), and compare with stratified sampling, which Aioli found hard to beat.
Go deeper. Data mixing, curricula and continued-pretraining ratios: DoReMi step by step, a mixing-law fitter on RegMix's 1,088 released runs, the token-budget planner, the Pile weightings compared, and the proxy experiment's full design. On the training side: Topic: llm-training-and-post-training.

Post-training data is small, structured and mostly written by other models. This lab opens four real samples, one per kind of data, measures them, runs a simple quality filter and three checks on them, and shows the same web page before and after a model rewrites it.

In one screenFour samplesA simple filterAnswer checkersRephrasingContaminationMistakes and questionsMethod

In one screen

  • A filter that looks safe can delete a skill. Ai2's own clean-up filters for the Tulu 3 SFT mixture remove of our 5,000 SFT rows. The two "obvious" extra rules would remove far more, and they would remove the wrong rows: an English-only rule takes rows, of them from the deliberately multilingual Aya subset. A rule against refusal phrases takes rows, of them from the two safety subsets whose whole job is to teach refusals.
  • One preference pair in nine carries no preference. In UltraFeedback binarized, of 5,000 pairs give the chosen and the rejected answer the same judge score: the "rejected" answer was drawn at random from the other completions, and ties were allowed. In more pairs the two texts are identical. Chosen answers are also longer more often than not ( pairs): a model trained on these pairs can learn length.
  • A reward checker can make a prompt impossible to win. In Tulu 3's RLVR set, GSM8K labels are written with a thousands comma ("3,380"), while Tulu 3's checker strips commas from the answer before an exact string match, so no answer can score. Reference solutions show how checkers disagree: the last-number rule accepts of correct MATH solutions, math-verify .
  • Contamination hides at the level of one subject. The same RLVR set contains 70 MMLU test questions word for word (71 rows), all high-school maths, which is 0.50% of MMLU and so passes Tulu 3's 2% rule (measured by the Decontamination child page; the checker below re-scores its pairs).
  • Generating from a seed is not rephrasing. A Cosmopedia document keeps almost none of its seed web page's wording (median of its 4-word sequences are new, as long) and the FineWeb-Edu classifier's pass rate goes from . WRAP-style rephrasing with Qwen3-4B keeps the content and changes the form (section 5).

Four samples, one per kind of data

Each stage of post-training (explained in Reading, section 9 and, for how the data is used, on Alignment: SFT, RLHF, DPO Family, RLVR) eats a different shape of row. The samples were drawn by the setup step (see the root's src/data/README.md); a sample's shares are not the full mixture's: the Tulu 3 SFT sample holds 1,000 rows from each of five subsets, while the full mixture has 939,344 rows from many more (Tulu 3, Table 7). Lengths are counted in Qwen3 tokens.

Length of one row

Rows from the sample

Short excerpts of real rows, chosen by reading to show each kind of row and each rule that fires. Rows from WildChat (real user conversations) and the adversarial safety subsets are shown only where the prompt is harmless; they count in every statistic.

A simple quality filter, before and after

The problem. Distilled and crowd-sourced rows carry junk: a teacher model announcing it is ChatGPT, a "knowledge cutoff" sentence, a response stuck in a loop, the same conversation twice. How it works. Cheap rules, applied in order, each removing what it matches. The text rules here are Ai2's own clean-up scripts for the Tulu 3 SFT mixture, run unchanged from open-instruct (commit 72f46040): filter_dataset_by_keywords.py (model and provider names in assistant turns, PATTERNS lines 45 to 105), filter_cutoff_date.py (CUT_OFF_PATTERN lines 17 to 37) and filter_ngram_repetitions.py (repeated blocks or sentences, lines 679 to 694). The other rules are defined here and named as such. The cost is a regex per row; the risk is what the rules take that you wanted.

How to check a filter like this: count what each rule removes per subset, then read what it removed. On this sample the identity rule fires on refusals in the WildGuardMix subset that say "As an AI developed by OpenAI" (row examples above); the cutoff rule checks every message, so one sentence in any turn of a long WildChat conversation removes the whole conversation.

Answer checkers: when is an answer right?

An RLVR row is a prompt plus a checker: a program that extracts the final answer from the model's response and compares it with the stored label. The reward is only as good as both halves. Six ways to extract and compare, run on every GSM8K and MATH row of Tulu 3's RLVR set against the reference solution of the same problem (GSM8K and MATH training splits, joined on the question text: rows): a correct checker should accept all of them.

Where they disagree, on real reference solutions

The same web page before and after rephrasing

Two ways to turn web text into synthetic training text (Reading, section 8): rephrase it (WRAP: keep the content, change the style) or generate from it (Cosmopedia: use the page as a seed for a new textbook section or blog post). Pick a document and a style; the animation rewrites the source into the output. Words in a 4-word sequence that also occurs in the source turn green; numbers from the source that survive are kept, the rest struck through.

in a 4-word sequence copied from the sourcenew wordingsource number missing from the output

Cosmopedia: seed page against generated document, FineWeb-Edu classifier score

A contamination checker over real rows

The problem: a training row that contains a test question makes the test score a memory test. How it works: both texts are normalised (lower-case, punctuation to spaces; datatrove's simplify_text, numbers kept), cut into word n-grams, and compared. GPT-3 flagged any shared 13-gram; Tulu 3 flags a test item when more than 50% of its tokens sit inside 8-grams shared with one training row, and removes a training set that overlaps more than 2% of a benchmark (Tulu 3 paper, decontamination). The rows and items below are real pairs that some rule flagged, labelled by reading on the Decontamination child page; the matching runs live here with that page's normalisation, so its numbers and these agree.

Benchmark item (question underlined, then its answer), highlighted where covered
Training row, the region holding every shared 8- and 13-gram (at shorter n, matches outside it are not counted)
Predict: Tulu 3's rule removes a training set that overlaps more than 2% of a benchmark's items. Would it remove the RLVR set for MMLU, given the 70 copied questions?
No. The threshold is per benchmark, and MMLU has 14,042 test items, so 70 copies are 0.50%. Inside the one subject they come from, high-school mathematics, they are 26% of the items. A per-row filter (drop any training row that covers a test item) would have removed all 71 rows; a per-dataset threshold keeps them all.
Counts from the Decontamination child page's scan (its scripts/dg_contam.py and hand labels), 29,615 benchmark items: MMLU, GSM8K, ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, HumanEval, MATH-500, HellaSwag. Labels are an agent's reading, not a human annotator's.

Common mistakes

Filtering a mixture with one rule for all subsets
Rules that are right for one subset are wrong for another: "drop refusals" is right for a helpfulness subset and destroys a safety subset; "English only" deletes the multilingual one; "drop near-duplicate prompts" on RLVR's instruction-following rows would remove rows that share a base prompt but carry different constraints (the largest such cluster holds 16 rows). Count removals per subset before running anything.
Training on ties
A preference pair whose two answers got the same score teaches nothing true, and a pair with identical texts teaches noise. Check the score margin distribution of any preference set; UltraFeedback binarized has ties in this sample.
Trusting a checker you have not run on correct answers
Run the checker on reference solutions first: every rejection is a false negative the RL run will push against. Here a label format (a thousands comma) makes GSM8K prompts unwinnable under Tulu 3's checker, and the strict Minerva checker accepts many correct MATH solutions only by accident (its fallback normalises the whole response).
Reading a sample's mix as the dataset's mix
This page's SFT sample is 1,000 rows from each of five subsets; percentages here describe the sample. Recompute on the full mixture before quoting a share.

Interview questions

Design the data pipeline for an SFT mixture of one million rows.
Sources per skill (curated prompts, distilled responses, safety, multilingual), each with its licence; per-source cleaning (identity and cutoff strings, repetition, empty or truncated turns); exact then near dedup of prompts within and across sources; decontamination of prompts against every evaluation you will report (n-gram plus an embedding pass for paraphrases), with per-row removal, not only a dataset threshold; length limits matched to the training context; per-subset counts and a read sample at every step; and an ablation per subset, because quality is measured by the model trained on it.
How do you build a preference dataset, and what can go wrong?
Sample several responses per prompt (from a pool of models, or on-policy from the model being trained), score them with a judge or reward model, pair a better with a worse one. Failure modes: ties and tiny margins (noise), judge biases (length, style, position) that the pairs pass on, off-policy pairs that the model would never produce, and contaminated prompts.
What makes a good verifiable-reward prompt?
A label in a canonical form, a checker tested on correct and incorrect answers in the formats the model will actually use, a difficulty where the model sometimes succeeds (always or never solved teaches nothing), and no overlap with the evaluations.

Which tool for which job

The rules are judgement built from the facts in the atlas (each tool name opens its card); they encode the usual trade-off: CPU stages are cheap per document and run on everything, GPU stages are expensive and run only on what survives.

Corpus lineage: who built on whom

Each dot is a public corpus at its first public release, placed by date; a line means the later corpus was built from the earlier one (a filter, a dedup or a mix). A small CC mark means it was extracted directly from Common Crawl. Play the years to watch the field move from mixes of curated sources (The Pile, RedPajama) to filtered web (RefinedWeb, FineWeb, DCLM), then to model-scored and rephrased web (FineWeb-Edu, Nemotron-CC) and licence-clean sets (Common Corpus, Common Pile). Then switch to today: the same corpora coloured by what you can download now and under which terms.

Licences: what a corpus lets you do

Three layers of rights stack on every web corpus: the original pages' copyright (which no dataset licence can waive), Common Crawl's Terms of Use for the crawl itself, and the dataset's own licence for the compilation (the selection, cleaning and metadata). ODC-By (Open Data Commons Attribution) licenses only the compilation and asks for attribution; it says nothing about the pages inside. Gated datasets add a click-through agreement on top. The table reads each licence verbatim from the Hugging Face card metadata (fetched ); it is not legal advice.

Same input, two toolkits: datatrove and the Dolma toolkit

The atlas says datatrove filters inline and the Dolma toolkit tags, then mixes. To see what that means, the same twelve small documents go through both. They are illustrative: written for this test (no real pages), each built to trip one rule: an exact copy, a near copy, a banner, a repeated line, German text, hashtag spam, a menu, lorem ipsum, an email address, a code fragment, and two clean articles. The runs are measured: both libraries' real code, at the versions shown.

Storage and loading: from documents to what the trainer reads

A finished corpus is stored twice. First as documents (text plus metadata) in Parquet or compressed JSONL, so it can be inspected, filtered again and published. Then, after tokenization, as token shards: one flat array of token ids per file plus an index of where each document ends, which the training loader memory-maps and cuts into fixed-length windows. The second form is what a pretraining run actually reads.

Packing lays documents end to end into fixed-length windows instead of one document per padded window: on these 2,000 documents almost every position becomes real text (the numbers are in the loader note below). Storage and loading at scale, section 6, owns it: a placement stepper on the same documents, attention per window and document masks. This tab's packing stepper was retired on 2026-10-24.

Go deeper: Storage and loading at scale covers formats, compression levels, shard sizes and training loaders in depth, and reproduces these sizes.

Interview questions

You must build a 10T-token English web corpus in two months with 2,000 CPU cores and 64 GPUs. Which tools, and where do the GPUs go?
CPU stages run on everything, cheapest first: WARC reading, extraction (resiliparse rather than trafilatura at this scale: DCLM measured about 8 times the speed with similar downstream scores), lid.176, heuristic rules, and MinHash within each crawl, all as datatrove tasks on the CPU cluster. GPUs only score what survives: a FineWeb-Edu-style classifier or an ensemble, and optionally rephrasing. Then tokenize to .bin shards. Say what you would measure first: drop counts per stage on one crawl before running all of them.
Why would a team keep the Dolma toolkit's tag-then-mix design rather than inline filters?
Tagging writes every score once; changing a threshold then only reruns the cheap mixer, not the expensive taggers. Inline filters (datatrove's default) are simpler and stream, but a new threshold means a new pass (unless the filters write their scores to metadata). At web scale the ability to re-mix without re-tagging is worth the extra storage for attribute files.
Exact Bloom-filter dedup and MinHash disagree on the toy near copy. Which is right?
Neither is wrong; they answer different questions. Measured above: the Dolma toolkit's paragraph-level Bloom dedup removed d03's six repeated paragraphs and kept its one reworded sentence as a document; datatrove's document-level MinHash removed d03 whole. For training, a page that differs only in a footer adds almost nothing, so MinHash's choice is usually what you want; paragraph dedup also strips repeated boilerplate inside otherwise unique pages. Many pipelines do both.
Your vocabulary has 151,000 tokens. What changes in storage?
Token ids no longer fit in 16 bits (65,536 values), so shards need uint32: twice the bytes per token. datatrove's DocumentTokenizer has token_size 2 by default; set it to 4. A silent uint16 write would wrap ids and corrupt training data without an error.
Name a tool on this map that is archived but still everywhere, and say why that is fine or not.
fastText: the repository is read-only since 2024, yet lid.176 still runs language ID for most English corpora. Fine for inference of a frozen model with a pinned wheel; not fine if you need fixes or new platforms (the community forks such as fasttext-numpy2 exist for exactly that). Same pattern for the suffix-array code: the method lives on in datatrove and Dolma 3's tools.
